background.definition: Sexual dysfunctions are characterized by distubrbances in sexual desire and in the psychophysiological changes associated with the sexual response cycle (desire, excitement, orgasm, resolution) that cause marked distress and interpersonal difficulty. There are four major types of female sexual dysfunction: (1) disorder of desire (hypodesire, hyperdesire, global desire, and situational desire); (2) disorder of arousal; (3) sex pain (dyspareunia and vaginismus); and (4) orgasmic disorders (primary and secondary, during masturbation or coitus, situational or partner specific).

list.listitem: A population study of 1749 women in the United States found a 43% prevalence of female sexual dysfunction; 22% had low desire, 14% had arousal problems, and 7% had sexual pain.
Desire disorders are the chief complaint of 30% to 55% of individual female patients presenting to clinics, and 31% of couples.

Other estimates of female dysfunction range from 19% to 50% in primary care outpatient populations and increase to 68% to 75% when sexual dissatisfaction or problems (not dysfunctional in nature) are included.

Estimated prevalence of postpartum dyspareunia was 35% (95% confidence interval [CI], 29%-41%) based on a meta-analysis of 22 observational studies including 11,457 women. Prevalence decreased from 42% at 2 months to 22% at 6 to 12 months postpartum.

Primary care patients often fail to disclose symptoms of an intimate or personal nature to their physicians. In one study, among 139 patients who identified an intention to discuss at least one symptom from a checklist with their physician, 43 patients failed to disclose 67 symptoms including stress, worries, sleep problems, urinary problems, headache and intimate or personal problems during the visit.
Conflict regarding intimacy.
Religious taboos.
Sexual identity conflicts.
Past or current sexual, physical, or verbal abuse.
Depression, anxiety, or life stressors are commonly associated with sexual dysfunction.
Drug use, including prescription medications (aromatase inhibitors, topiramate, MAO inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, beta-blockers, especially SSRI antidepressants) and chemotherapy.
Change in desire or arousal during or following pregnancy.
Chronic illness (diabetic vascular disease, hypertension, thyroid disease, arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosis, urinary or bowel difficulties, renal disease, multiple sclerosis, cancer).
Sexual inexperience.
Partner sexual dysfunction.
Negative body perception.
Spinal cord injury.
Cancer treatment.
Urogenital or vaginal atrophy.
Cycling-related female sexual dysfunction.
There is an association with diabetes, but it is poorly understood, with BMI an important confounder.
Perineal trauma during childbirth (but not mode of delivery) increases the likelihood of sexual dysfunction in the first year following childbirth.

Vascular causes: diminished blood flow to the pelvic region due to a medical condition, aging, stress, or hypoactive sexual desire causes reduced sensitivity (particularly of the clitoris), dryness, and impaired arousal.
Hormonal causes: inadequate or decreased levels of estrogen and testosterone, caused by aging.
Dissatisfaction theory: interpersonal and intrapersonal problems lead to decreased desire, fear of intimacy, and/or the inability to adequately stimulate the genitals.
Establish the patient's sexual orientation. C
Conduct a thorough patient history with an emphasis on interpersonal relationship dynamics and psychosocial stressors (such as sexual abuse). C
Conduct a thorough gynecologic examination. C

list.listitem: Desire disorder: Persistently or recurrently deficient (or absent) sexual fantasies and desire for sexual activity. The judgment of deficiency or absences made by the provider must take into account factors that affect sexual functioning, such as age and the context of the person's life.
Arousal disorder: Persistent or recurrent inability to attain, or to maintain until completion of the sexual activity, an adequate lubrication-swelling response to sexual excitement.

Orgasmic disorder: Persistent or recurrent delay in, or absence of, orgasm, following a normal sexual excitement phase. The diagnosis of the disorder should be based on the provider's judgment that the woman's orgasmic capacity is less then would be reasonable for her age, sexual experience, and adequacy of sexual stimulation.

Pain disorder: Recurrent or persistent genital pain associated with sexual intercourse (dyspareunia). Recurrent or persistent involuntary spasm of the musculature of the outer third of the vagina that interferes with sexual intercourse (vaginismus). Dyspareunia is divided into 3 types: superficial, vaginal, or deep. Superficial pain occurs with attempted penetration, usually secondary to anatomic or irritative conditions, or vaginismus. Vaginal pain is related to friction (ie, lubrication problems). Deep pain is related to thrusting, often associated with pelvic disease or relaxation. Vaginismus is often related to past abuse or trauma and/or sexual phobias.

Determine the onset and duration of the dysfunction and determine whether the dysfunction occurs with a specific partner, in a certain setting, or in a definable circumstance. Ask the patient what they believe is causing the problem and her expectations of treatment.
A routine examination should look for signs of general medical conditions, such as diabetes mellitus or thyroid disease.

Each patient should undergo a thorough gynecologic examination guided by and tailored to patient comfort. The examination provides an opportunity to educate the patient about normal anatomy and sexual function, and to reproduce and localize pain encountered during sexual activity. The examination begins with inspection of the external genitalia, including a cotton swab test, if indicated.

For patients with dyspareunia, a mono-manual examination should follow. The timing of the speculum examination should be guided by patient symptoms. In patients with deep dyspareunia, the speculum examination should follow the bimanual examination because localization of pain is crucial in these patients. The focus should be on recreating the pain. In patients in whom vaginitis, cervical cancer, or a sexually transmitted disease is suspected, cultures and vaginal samples should be obtained first.
Diagnosis of an underlying etiology should be sought, and laparoscopy may be considered for pain disorder.
summarizes signs and symptoms of female sexual dysfunction and their possible causes.
lists validated case-finding questions to identify women with sexual dysfunction.
Laboratory testing should be guided by patient symptoms and examination findings. No specific tests are universally recommended for patients with sexual dysfunction.
Conduct an endocrine assessment (testosterone, prolactin, FSH, LH, and TSH).
Conduct vaginal pH testing to detect bacteria-causing vaginitis as a cause of dyspareunia.

Use the PLISSIT model: gain "Permission" to discuss sexual problems; give "Limited Information" to the patient about normal sexual response cycle; make "Specific Suggestions" that are directly related to the patient's particular sexual complaint; and recommend "Intensive Therapy" with a sexual health specialist and/or marriage and family therapist.
Rule in or rule out gynecologic causes and psychological causes manifesting as a sexual disorder.

Prescribe HT for desire and arousal disorders; transdermal is more effective.B
Consider HT for perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with desire or arousal disorders. C
It is common for patients to need both medical and mental health treatment. C

Drug therapy is generally less effective and should be used with or after psychotherapy. If no etiology is discovered, educate the patient (see Patient Education section of this chapter) and consider a referral for counseling.

ACOG guidelines recommend vaginal estrogen for patients with genitourinary syndrome of menopause, characterized by vaginal dryness, decreased lubrication, and resultant dyspareunia. Options include: 17 beta estradiol cream 0.5 to 1 gm twice weekly Conjugated estrogen cream 0.5 gm twice weekly 17-beta estradiol vaginal ring (2 mg), device releases 7.5 mcg/day for 90 days Estradiol vaginal troche (4 mcg or 10 mcg), 1 troche twice weekly Estradiol hemihydrate vaginal tablets (10 mcg), 1 tablet twice weekly Alternatives to estrogen: Prasterone vaginal troche 6.5 gm, 1 troche daily; or raloxifene 60 mg once daily

A randomized trial compared a combined oral contraceptive (150 mcg levonorgestrel and 30 mg estradiol) with placebo in 340 Swedish women. Of 7 domains in a sexual function scale, three were worsened (desire, pleasure, and arousal) while 4 were unaffected (orgasm, concern, responsiveness, and self-image). Another study found that change to a nonandrogenic or androgenic progestin containing OCP did not have any effect on sexual function.

In a small randomized crossover trial, intranasal oxytocin given an hour before intercourse was no better than placebo for women with sexual dysfunction. This was confirmed by a systematic review of 7 studies of oxytocin gel which also found no benefit.

A small Thai trial randomized 67 women meeting criteria for female sexual dysfunction to intravaginal conjugated estrogen tablets or placebo for 12 weeks. There were changes in vaginal pH but no changes in any measures of sexual function.

listitem.strong: Disorders of desire (hypoactive sexual desire disorder or HSDD)

list.listitem: The use of transdermal hormone therapy (HT) correlates positively with sexual activity, enjoyment, and fantasies. The mechanism is thought to be mediated by an improvement in urogenital atrophy, reduction in vasomotor symptoms, and improvement in menopausal mood disorders. Several RCTs of HT or sildenafil have shown a positive effect on sexual dysfunction in both perimenopausal and postmenopausal women.

Although low testosterone levels do not cause sexual dysfunction in most women, transdermal testosterone replacement (1 gm of a 1% cream) can be effective in improving sexual function and is recommended by ACOG guidelines (2024). Testosterone may have a slight benefit in postmenopausal women with low sexual desire, but there is probably a large placebo effect. In one study of postmenopausal women, a 300-mcg testosterone patch applied daily modestly improved libido but there were several cases of breast cancer in the intervention groups which raised some concern. A similar effect is seen in women with impaired sexual function after oophorectomy.
Transdermal testosterone did not improve sexual desire in women cancer survivors.
Flibanserin in a dose of 50 or 100 mg led to statistically significant changes in some measures of sexual function, but their clinical significance is highly questionable.

Bremelanotide, a melanocortin receptor agonist administered as a subcutaneous injection approximately 45 minutes prior to sexual activity, was approved by the FDA in 2019. Two RCTs randomized a total of 1267, of whom 1202 were in the efficacy population. The primary outcome was satisfying sexual events within 16 hours and was no different between groups (difference of 0.0 events comparing end to beginning of study). There were small improvements in some sexual function scales that were of questionable clinical significance. Exit surveys with 242 participants from these trials, including 80 who also completed qualitative telephone interviews, demonstrated some improvements in physical arousal, quality of sexual relationships and communication with their partner not seen in patients taking placebo.
Current treatment of patients with arousal disorder is limited to the use of commercial lubricants (eg, Viagel), although vitamin E and mineral oils are also options.
Arousal disorders may be secondary to inadequate stimulation, especially in older women. Patient education regarding stimulation and foreplay may increase arousal.
For postmenopausal women, urogenital atrophy is the most common cause of arousal disorders. Estrogen therapy, when appropriate, is usually the most effective therapy.

A study randomized 200 women with female sexual arousal disorder to topic sildenafil cream or placebo cream. There was no significant difference between groups for the primary outcome. Some post-hoc analyses showed some favorable results but require confirmation.
Treatment of the underlying etiology is fundamental, but long-term pain management strategies should also be taught. NSAIDs before intercourse can be tried, but clinical trial data are lacking.

Authors of a network meta-analysis identified 5 studies with 275 patients comparing therapies for vestibulodynia. They concluded that oral desipramine with or without topical lidocaine was the most effective treatment option, but the size and quality of included studies was limited.
Evidence from several RCTs indicates that topical estrogen relieves vaginal dryness and dyspareunia in postmenopausal women.

In an RCT of 60 symptomatic postmenopausal women, a vaginal gel (Meclon Idra), containing sea buckthorn oil, aloe vera, 18β-glycyrrhetic acid, hyaluronic acid and glycogen, was effective in reducing vaginal pain, dyspareunia and vaginal pH at day 90, and reduced vaginal symptoms (dryness, itching and burning) at weeks 2 and 4, and the end of the study.

There is limited evidence that lubricating creams reduce sexual dysfunction after radiotherapy among women being treated for cervical cancer. A pH-balanced vaginal gel was helpful in women with sexual dysfunction who had been treated for cancer.

A systematic review of 31 RCTs identified 4 interventions more effective than placebo for endometriosis related pelvic pain: leuprolide, leuprolide combined with oral contraceptive pills (OCPs), dienogest, and combined OCPs. The most effective treatments for dyspareunia were elagolix and the combination of vitamin C and vitamin E.
Multispecialty guidelines (2025) conclude that the evidence is strongest for low dose topical vaginal estrogen creams for the treatment of genitourinary syndrome of menopause.
A Cochrane review of 35 studies concluded that estrogen alone "probably slightly improves sexual function"; a similar effect was not seen for estrogen + progestins.
A systematic review of 46 RCTs concluded that vaginal DHEA, vaginal estrogen, oral ospemifene, and vaginal moisturizers were likely effective for dyspareunia treatment, at least in the short-term.

In a study of 98 women age 18 to 50 years with antidepressant associated sexual dysfunction, sildanefil provided modest benefit (about 1 point on a 7 point scale). Another RCT found a small difference in a rating scale of sexual dysfunction in women with antidepressant-induced sexual dysfunction randomized to sildenafil.
A study of women with antidepressant-related sexual dysfunction found that transdermal testosterone increased the number of satisfactory sexual events.
Treatment for chronic pelvic pain is discussed in that chapter.
Authors of a systematic review found similar rates of dyspareunia following transvaginal prolapse repair between mesh or graft versus native tissue repair.

Labiaplasty for labia minora hypertrophy was associated with increased enjoyment and decreased pain in a small quasi-experimental study comparing 12 patients with immediate surgery with 12 who had delayed surgery.
A prospective cohort study in 86 specialist centers in the UK found that hysterectomy with or without oophorectomy were more effective for treatment of dyspareunia.
A narrative review found no evidence to support the use of herbal remedies for female sexual dysfunction.

A small Iranian study with 74 women found a possible benefit to saffron 15 mg (Crocus sativus) twice daily compared with placebo. The improvement at 6 weeks was of borderline statistical significance (p = 0.05) and clinical significance (4 point greater improvement on a 36-point scale).

Another small Iranian study randomized 96 postmenopausal women with sexual dysfunction to chamomile vaginal gel, conjugated estrogen vaginal cream, or placebo cream. Chamomile gel resulted in a similar improvement compared with estrogen and a greater improvement than with placebo gel. The small study, uncertain masking, and short-term follow-up are important limitations.
Two small studies provide no clear evidence to support the use of tribulus terrestris for hypoactive sexual desire disorder.
In an RCT of 80 women with sexual dysfunction, celery seed compared to placebo improved sexual desire, arousal, lubrication, and pain at 6 weeks.
In an RCT with 41 women age 30 to 60 years with metabolic syndrome, a yoga intervention improved measures of arousal and lubrication compared with a wait-listed control group.

Investigators randomized 67 women with endometriosis pain to psychotherapy plus somatosensory stimulation using acupuncture point stimulation or wait-list control. Pain and quality of life outcomes were improved in the intervention group, although there was not a statistically significant improvement in dyspareunia (−1.8 points; 95% CI, −4.4 to 0.7).

A systematic review of the vasodilator visnadine (from Bishop's Weed) found only 2 RCTs with 97 patients. Both studies found a benefit but more data are needed to fully assess potential benefits and harms.

Standard treatment of vaginismus consists of progressive muscle relaxation and vaginal dilation. Progressive muscle relaxation can be taught during an instructional examination by having the patient alternate contracting and relaxing the pelvic muscles around the examiner's finger. Women with vaginismus can achieve vaginal dilation with the use of commercial dilators of tampons of increasing diameter, placed in the vagina for 15 minutes twice daily. Once the patient can easily accept an equivalent-sized dilator into the vagina, penile penetration by the partner can occur.

A German study randomized 300 primiparous women 6 months after delivery to 6 weeks of pelvic floor muscle training for 45 minutes once weekly or no intervention. At 12 months, there was no difference between groups in pelvic floor strength or sexual function, which improved in both groups. The study is limited by the large number of dropouts (n=100) and the minimal nature of the once-weekly intervention.

In an RCT of 212 women with provoked vestibulodynia, randomization to 10-weeks of weekly multimodal physical therapy was more effective than overnight topical lidocaine for reducing pain intensity during intercourse at both post-treatment and 6 months. In addition, the former group had greater improvement in pain quality, sexual function, sexual distress, satisfaction, and participants' impression of change.

In an RCT of 77 postmenopausal women, of whom 51 (73%) had sexual dysfunction according to the Female Sexual Function Index questionnaire, there were no significant differences in domain scores between those who underwent supervised home pelvic-floor muscle training and the control group. However, fewer women in the intervention group met criteria for sexual dysfunction at the end of the study (20/35 vs. 24/29 in the control group).

In a feasibility study of 31 cancer survivors with dyspareunia, participation in 12 weekly 60-min physical therapy sessions combining education, manual therapy, pelvic floor muscle exercises using biofeedback and home exercises (which included the use of a dilator), resulted in improvement in all symptoms including pain intensity, pain quality, sexual function, pelvic floor dysfunction symptoms and quality of life.
For orgasmic disorders, treatment based on expert opinion involves maximizing stimulation and minimizing inhibition.

A study randomized 114 women with polycystic ovary syndrome to continuous oral contraceptive pill, intensive lifestyle modification, or both. No group saw an improvement in the total Female Sexual Function Index. However, most women did not meet diagnostic criteria for sexual dysfunction.

Authors of a systematic review found 15 trials of psychological therapies for female sexual dysfunction. The most common approaches were based on cognitive behavioral therapy or the teaching of Masters and Johnson, and both approaches were generally effective.

A study randomized 106 women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder to CBT for 8 weeks or waiting list control. At 6 months, the CBT group had statistically and clinically significant improvements compared to control in domains of desire and interest, excitement and attunement, and orgasm and satisfaction. Smaller improvements were seen for foreplay and comfort.
A small trial found that Internet-based psychological treatment led to improvement in measures of sexual and relationship function compared with no treatment.

In an RCT of 148 women with sexual interest/arousal disorder, similar improvement in desire and arousal were demonstrated following both the mindfulness-based cognitive therapy plus sex education group and supportive sex education and therapy group, with 12-month retention of improvements.

Authors of a Cochrane review found 8 studies of behavioral interventions in women with sexual dysfunction after cancer treatment. Three found a benefit and five did not, most were at high risk of bias.
An uncontrolled study of 46 ovarian cancer survivors found benefit from sexual health education, cognitive behavioral therapy and relaxation training after up to 6 months follow-up.
Couples therapy with a licensed marriage and family therapist with a specialization in sex therapy is the preferred approach.
For patients with sexual abuse, individual therapy with a mental health professional with a specialization in trauma and abuse can be used as a secondary approach.

Both biofeedback and electrical stimulation were effective in improving Female Sexual Function Index scores for 22 patients with sexual dysfunction and stress incontinence, although women in the biofeedback group benefited more than those receiving electrical stimulation with respect to desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, and satisfaction scores.
Twice-repeated injections of botulinum toxin vs. placebo, given 3 months apart in women with provoked vestibulodynia did not reduce dyspareunia or pain at tampon use.

Authors of a systematic review of laser therapy for genitourinary syndrome of menopause with or without incontinence found statistically significant differences in dryness, dyspareunia, and urinary symptoms. However, the 14 small studies were of low or very low quality, so these results must be interpreted very cautiously.
Arousal and orgasmic disorders can typically be treated within 6 months.
Pain disorders typically require 6 months to 1 year of treatment.
Reasons to refer include: longstanding dysfunction; multiple dysfunctions; current or past abuse; psychological disorders, or acute psychological event; unknown etiology; and no response to therapy.
Lack of desire is most difficult to treat (less than 50% successful by patient report). C
Arousal and orgasmic disorders are quite responsive to therapy (approximately 75% success rate by patient report). C
Pain disorder treatment success has been reported to be as high as 90% for vaginismus. B
Provide reassurance regarding the sexual response cycle, normal anatomy, and sexual function. Dispel the common myth that most women have orgasms during intercourse.
Educate about enhancing stimulation and eliminating routines. Discuss vibrators, foreplay, varying sexual positions and times of day or places, and suggest making a "date" for sexual activity.

Educate about distraction techniques. Recommend pelvic muscle contraction and relaxation exercises (similar to Kegel exercises) with intercourse and recommend the use of background music, videos, or television.

Educate about noncoital behaviors. Recommend sensual massage and sensate-focus (sensual massage with no involvement of sexual areas, where one partner provides the massage and the receiving partner provides feedback as to what feels good; aimed at promoting comfort and communication between partners). Recommend oral or noncoital stimulation, with or without orgasm.

Educate about minimizing dyspareunia. For superficial pain: female astride for control of penetration, topical lidocaine, warm baths before intercourse, and biofeedback. For vaginal pain: same as for superficial pain, but with the addition of lubricants. For deep pain: position changes so that force is away from pain and deep thrusts are minimized.
The Female Sexual Function Index, a 19-item validated measure of sexual function, can be used to assess improvements from therapy or over time.

Lower estrogen levels during menopausal transition may lead to changes in genital tissues and sexual responsiveness. Also, the decreased elasticity and thinning of the vagina causes the vagina to become narrower and more susceptible to painful intercourse. Decreased lubrication in the vagina leads to potential arousal disorders and painful intercourse. In these cases, vaginal estrogen therapy should be considered.
Several empirical studies confirm HT for perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with arousal or desire sexual dysfunctions.

tr.td: Assess pubic hair amount and distribution
Assess posterior fourchette and hymenal ring
Urethritis, interstitial cystitis, urinary tract infection

feature.caption: Suggested screening questions for identifying women with sexual problems

tr.th: Ask: In the past 12 months, has there been a period of at least 3 months when you had any of the following?

tr.td: You wanted to feel more interest in sexual activity
You had pain during or after sexual activity
You had difficulty having an orgasm
You felt anxious about sexual activity
You did not enjoy sexual activity
You had some other sexual problem or concern
